text.definition: Trimmed text. Required values cannot be blank or placeholders.

yes_no_unknown.definition: Use yes, no, unknown, or not_applicable.

choice.definition: Use one exact allowed value from the question.

questions.prompt: What is the project name?
questions.definition: The human-readable working name used in registers, reports, approvals, and generated files.
questions.follow_up: What short name would you use in a status meeting?
invalid_examples: Project

questions.prompt: Which company owns or sponsors this work?
questions.definition: The legal entity, business unit, or organization accountable for the work.
questions.follow_up: Which organization would own the deliverable and records?
invalid_examples: me
unknown

questions.prompt: Who is accountable for final project decisions?
questions.definition: The named person accountable for project outcomes and reserved decisions. The owner may delegate work but remains accountable.
questions.follow_up: Who can approve scope, funding, acceptance, and closure?
invalid_examples: the team
AI

questions.prompt: Is this temporary work with a defined outcome and finish condition?
questions.definition: Temporary work has a specific objective, a beginning, an ending or exit condition, and a distinct deliverable or result.
questions.follow_up: What exact outcome would let the work be declared complete?
invalid_examples: sometimes
yes because we always do it

questions.prompt: Is this recurring operational work expected to continue indefinitely?
questions.definition: Operational work is repeatable, ongoing activity that sustains the business and has no planned project end.
questions.follow_up: After the requested change is complete, will the same work continue as a routine cycle?
invalid_examples: yes, build the new system

questions.prompt: What concrete outcome or deliverable must exist?
questions.definition: A result stated as an observable deliverable or changed condition, not merely an activity.
questions.follow_up: What will be different when this work is finished?
valid_examples: A validated execution policy, work-order compiler, and controlled pilot report.
invalid_examples: Work on autonomy.
Make it better.

questions.prompt: How will success be measured or accepted?
questions.definition: The objective evidence, metric, acceptance criterion, or approval that proves the outcome is satisfactory.
questions.follow_up: What evidence would convince the owner to accept the result?
valid_examples: Node 20 and 22 pass all controls; a low-risk pilot work order completes with independent verification.
invalid_examples: It works.
Everyone likes it.

questions.prompt: What is the expected project duration?
questions.definition: The planned elapsed time from authorization to acceptance, not the total labor hours.
questions.follow_up: From authorization to acceptance, which duration band applies?
invalid_examples: quick
40 hours

questions.prompt: How many active contributors are expected?
questions.definition: People or autonomous agents assigned accountable work, excluding passive reviewers and observers.
questions.follow_up: How many people or agents will own work packages?
invalid_examples: small
the whole company

questions.prompt: Will an external client, customer, buyer, partner, or stakeholder see, approve, use, pay for, pilot, or rely on the result?
questions.definition: Client-facing means the work or output is delivered to or relied upon by an external party outside the internal builder group.
questions.follow_up: Who outside the internal project team will rely on this?
invalid_examples: yes because a coworker sees it

questions.prompt: Could the result be accessed or viewed outside a controlled private audience?
questions.definition: Public-facing means available to an unrestricted or broadly accessible audience without named private access.
questions.follow_up: Could an unknown viewer access it without being specifically invited?
invalid_examples: no, but it is on a public URL

questions.prompt: Will the result use or represent Top Shelf Service LLC identity?
questions.definition: Branded means using the company name, product names, logo, visual system, public voice, claims, or presentation standards.
questions.follow_up: Will an external viewer associate the result with Top Shelf?
invalid_examples: no because it is only a README

questions.prompt: Will the work create, change, deploy, validate, or maintain executable technology?
questions.definition: Software work includes code, scripts, APIs, applications, packages, infrastructure-as-code, database migrations, automation, or technical contracts tied to execution.
questions.follow_up: Will the repository contain executable or deployment-affecting changes?
invalid_examples: no because an AI writes the code

questions.prompt: Will the project collect, store, process, transmit, display, import, export, or derive data about real people?
questions.definition: User data includes identifiers, profiles, activity, messages, files, schedules, analytics, progress, location, financial, employment, or behavioral information tied to a person.
questions.follow_up: What real-person information will the project touch?
invalid_examples: no because emails are not sensitive

questions.prompt: Will the project handle sensitive, confidential, regulated, credential, financial, health, precise-location, or high-impact personal data?
questions.definition: Sensitive data is data whose exposure, misuse, or incorrect processing could materially harm a person or organization.
questions.follow_up: Which data elements would cause harm if exposed or changed?
invalid_examples: no because the database is private

questions.prompt: Does the solution require identity, login, sessions, private access, invitations, roles, or permission checks?
questions.definition: Authentication proves identity; authorization determines what an identified actor may access or do.
questions.follow_up: Does access differ between people or roles?
invalid_examples: no because everyone shares one password

questions.prompt: Will the project accept, calculate, record, reconcile, display, quote, invoice, subscribe, or financially commit money?
questions.definition: Payments and financial commitments include checkout, invoices, subscriptions, quotes, pricing obligations, provider charges, and revenue records.
questions.follow_up: Will anyone pay, be charged, quoted, invoiced, or financially committed?
invalid_examples: no because payment happens manually

questions.prompt: Will the result run persistently in a hosted environment for external access, scheduled operation, or live integrations?
questions.definition: Production hosting includes any persistent live endpoint, hosted application, scheduled worker, database, or integration used beyond a local development machine.
questions.follow_up: Will this run anywhere other than a local machine?
invalid_examples: no because it is only a demo

questions.prompt: Will the work modify an existing live system or production configuration?
questions.definition: A production change alters code, data, infrastructure, permissions, integrations, or configuration currently used by real users or operations.
questions.follow_up: Could the change affect a currently operating service?
invalid_examples: no because the change is small

questions.prompt: Could the work delete, overwrite, irreversibly transform, or make existing data unavailable?
questions.definition: A destructive data change can permanently remove or alter records, schemas, histories, backups, or access in a way that is not trivially reversible.
questions.follow_up: Can this work permanently change or remove existing records?
invalid_examples: no because a backup probably exists

questions.prompt: Will real people outside the build team use, test, observe, pilot, validate, or provide decision-relevant feedback?
questions.definition: Real-user or pilot work exposes the result to actual intended users or operating conditions before full release or acceptance.
questions.follow_up: Will any intended user interact with it before final release?
invalid_examples: no because it is only one user

questions.prompt: Does an external agreement, proposal, statement of work, service term, acceptance, or change order govern the work?
questions.definition: A client contract or SOW defines external scope, obligations, deliverables, acceptance, payment, or change authority.
questions.follow_up: Who outside the build team approves scope and acceptance?
invalid_examples: no because the agreement is in email

questions.prompt: Will the result persuade, sell, position, publicly explain, or shape perception of Top Shelf or a product?
questions.definition: Brand or public marketing includes sales copy, claims, positioning, public screenshots, proposals, landing pages, decks, and branded product surfaces.
questions.follow_up: Will this influence how an external person perceives Top Shelf?
invalid_examples: no because it is not an advertisement

questions.prompt: Is the buyer, user, problem, value, scope, willingness-to-pay, alternative, or proof standard still uncertain?
questions.definition: Discovery validation is required when material business or user assumptions lack evidence.
questions.follow_up: What evidence proves this is worth building now?
invalid_examples: no because the idea sounds good

questions.prompt: Will AI agents plan, implement, review, coordinate, validate, document, or maintain work?
questions.definition: Agent use means an AI system receives an assigned role, responsibility, work order, or decision-support duty.
questions.follow_up: Will an AI system receive assigned project responsibility?
invalid_examples: no because a human prompted it

questions.prompt: May an AI agent take material actions without case-by-case human approval?
questions.definition: Autonomous agents can claim work, modify systems, invoke tools, push changes, merge, deploy, spend, or communicate based on policy rather than per-action approval.
questions.follow_up: Can an agent perform any material action after receiving only policy authorization?
invalid_examples: no because a policy exists

questions.prompt: Can project cost, vendor performance, subscriptions, licenses, cloud spend, contractors, or margin affect delivery or decisions?
questions.definition: Budget and vendor tracking controls planned and actual cost, commitments, suppliers, limits, and financial exposure.
questions.follow_up: Which costs or vendors could affect delivery, pricing, or operations?
invalid_examples: no because the service is cheap

questions.prompt: Does delivery depend on an external provider, contractor, platform, API, hosting service, or supplier?
questions.definition: An external vendor is any outside organization or person whose product, service, access, performance, or terms affect delivery.
questions.follow_up: Which outside provider could block, change, or charge for delivery?
invalid_examples: no because the vendor is free

questions.prompt: Could the project create external spending or a financial commitment requiring owner approval?
questions.definition: Material external spending is any new or increased external commitment subject to the company's approval policy. Until a numeric threshold is approved, any new external commitment requires review.
questions.follow_up: Could this authorize or increase an external payment?
invalid_examples: no because the amount is unknown

questions.prompt: Is the work subject to law, regulation, contractual compliance, industry standard, court rule, or formal policy obligation?
questions.definition: Compliance work must satisfy an external or formally approved rule set whose violation has legal, contractual, financial, security, or operational consequences.
questions.follow_up: What external or formal rule must this work satisfy?
invalid_examples: no because the team is small

questions.prompt: Would reversing the change require significant downtime, data restoration, client coordination, cost, or manual repair?
questions.definition: A difficult-to-reverse change is not safely undone by a simple documented rollback with low operational impact.
questions.follow_up: What would be required to restore the prior accepted state?
invalid_examples: no because Git can revert code

questions.prompt: Could the work interrupt, replace, or materially change an existing business or technical process?
questions.definition: Operational impact exists when current users, staff, systems, schedules, controls, or service delivery may change.
questions.follow_up: Which current process or service could change?
invalid_examples: no because users will be trained

questions.prompt: Is this a new product, offer, customer segment, market, or materially new use case?
questions.definition: A new product or market lacks established delivery evidence for the specific offering and audience.
questions.follow_up: Has Top Shelf already delivered and validated this same offer for this audience?
invalid_examples: no because similar products exist
